Winslow, Ariz., Oct. 29.—On Nov. 1, new rates on coal, coke, charcoal and briquettes will go into effect on the Santa Fe railroad from Gallup, New Mexico, which will materially reduce the cost of this winter's fuel to the people of northern Arizona.

As a result of efforts put forth by the Arizona Corporation Commission, the Santa Fe railroad has put reduced rates into effect, but not satisfied that the reductions are as low as they should be, the commission has already forwarded to the Interstate Commerce Commission a complaint asking for still lower rates on coal.

Industrial plants and consumers in general throughout northern Arizona will be saved several thousand dollars on this year's shipments.

Recently the corporation commissioners began to study the coal rate situation from Gallup to Arizona points, deciding that the railroads should make material reductions for the benefit of consumers. Special to The Washington Herald 4

Richmond, April 8—Griffith's Washingtons played around the Richmond Colts of the Virginia League this afternoon, winning 2-0. Even Joe Boehling, the Richmond boy, doing the mound work for Washington in the last three innings refused to allow Richmond to secure a hit, and during the entire game Griffith's men were only able to garner two hits, widely scattered.

Walter Johnson twirled the first six innings, allowing the only hits of the game, while Boehling held forth three rounds. Boehling was given a hearty reception when he stepped into the box, and after acquitting himself as he did, his reception after the game was one that would have made the heart of an old timer hilarious. Besides striking out two men, Boehling furnished the hit that drove in Washington's first run.

Maths secured the first hit for Richmond, in the second inning, but the next time up he struck out, as he also did when he faced Boehling.

Verbout allowed five hits during the four innings he held forth, while Strain, local pitcher trying out for the Colts, allowed five hits in five innings, twirling a better game than did his predecessor, but he was unable to stem the tide, and every Washington man up had a hit to his credit.

Spencer, the recruit who featured with a three-base hit, left tonight for Roanoke, where he will join the Rochesters.

The Washingtons left for the Capital City tonight at 5:50.

Griffith's men, in prime condition, put up the same class of ball during the season that they did with a patched-up team to-day. They will make it hot for the other clubs in the circuit.

NEW YORK, Jan. 19.—An article on Germany and France, with Special Reference to the Moroccan Question, by Count von Bernstorff, German Ambassador at Washington, appears in the current issue of The Outlook. It is as follows:

The Moroccan question has passed out of its controversial stage and is now part of history, at that we are able to look back on it with an impartial spirit and to judge the aims and results of the German Government's action with fairness—a fairness which seemed to be sometimes lacking during the heat of the discussion.

It is well known that in 1904 England and France were contending with each other for supremacy in Morocco. Then followed the Anglo-French agreement of April, 1904, and in the fall of the same year a French banking syndicate contracted a new large loan with Morocco. Privileges of such importance were granted to this group of banks that the eventual fate of the Sultan's Empire seemed to be decided. Germany, however, intervened: the Emperor visited Tangier, and few months later the conference of Algeciras was held. In fair words it proclaimed the independence of Morocco and the sovereignty of the Sultan. It also created a multitude of provisions and stipulated the "open door" in Morocco. At the same time, however, police powers were granted to France and Spain in eight open Moroccan ports; furthermore, the treaty concerning the aforementioned loan was ratified with certain amendments. Above all, owing to the long Algero-Moroccan border line, the conference could not prevent French influences in Morocco from continuing and even increasing. On account of the wholly unsettled and untenable conditions in Morocco—which it is no use denying—opportunity for the exertion of French influence could not long be wanting. In fact, the occupation of Ujda and the bombardment as well as the occupation of Casablanca soon followed. All this could have been prevented only if Germany had been inclined to restore order in Morocco, and first to go to war, as would have been inevitable, with the powers hostile to such an act on her part. The course of events will always prove to be more powerful than the most perfectly worded treaty provisions, and the Algeciras Act could not expect to alter the fact that Morocco, and her inhabitants, no longer in themselves possessed the strength to reorganize their country. Some enthusiasts believed that Muley Hafid would be able to perform this task, but they soon had to recognize that, notwithstanding his skill and ability as a statesman, he did not have the power to bring about the necessary changes without foreign assistance.

For the German government there was therefore only one way open to protect German commercial interests in Morocco, viz. by securing France's protection of those interests. moment for Gov. John T. Hoffman. A
senator went to Mr. Hoffman and
urged him to use his influence to have

Governor Hoffman looked steadily
and sternly at the senator for a few
moments. He took the resolution
and read it over and over again then,
turning to the senator, he asked:

to the county courthouse commissioners

to him unnecessary to impute any dishonesty since the measure in

"Do you mean to impute dishonesty
to these public officers?"

Strong stated yesterday that the City Club of New York favors the appointment of a landscape designer for the Park Department of the boroughs of Manhattan and Richmond. has to meet it halfway. If we withdraw into ourselves, re-

The attitude of aloofness is barren, unproductive,
uninterested in the human race. Feel for it, or if it
is not for you, you must love the world—
grass or trees, highways or humanity—to get out
of it.

He that loses the world, loses it.

not always at hand, therefore much
of this valuable forage crop is lost or
indifferently cared for by following
a simple plan, however, this hay can
be cured, and kept in stacks without
losing any shattered leaves or having it mold, according to H. F. Green-
stead in the Farm and Home.


Set a pole in the ground where you
want a stack. Throw a little brush
around the pole to begin stacking,
then stack the pea vines as soon as
wilted around this pole, making the
stack not more than eight feet in
diameter. When you have reached a
height of four feet nail two strips
six feet long to the pole at right
angles, then begin stacking on these
and when you have piled on another
four feet nail another pair of the
strips. Don't get on the stack, as
your weight would break through.


When you reach the top, cover with
a stack cover or grass hay. In a day
or two the hay will settle, leaving
an air space under each of the sup-
ports so that air can circulate freely.
The hay will not mold and can be fed
from the stack. This plan is prac-
ticed successfully in the south, where
pea hay is a staple forage crop.

All the departments of the Utah National Guard met in the battery gymnasium last evening for their annual smoker and blowout. The programme arranged with much trouble included some of the best professional and amateur talent in the city, and all of the different contests were entertaining.

Easily the feature of the evening was the Japanese fencing exhibition in two matches. In this contest two Japanese heavily padded faced each other with huge bamboo cudgels about five feet in length.

The blows rained on each other, staggered both men nearly to unconsciousness. They seemed to enjoy the sport, however, and the crowd was happy. In the first of these matches Professor Kalayashi won from Iluyashi.

After ten minutes of fast work in the second, Ilayashi won handily. The other bouts of the evening were wrestling and boxing matches. Jack Downey of the Y. M. C. A. took on two of his pupils for two rounds each. Myers, the Y. M. C. A. candidate for lightweight amateur honours, showed up well against his instructor as also did Mc Donald, of the same class.

Wrestling was between Siddoway of Company III and Parker of the battery. Siddoway had his man outclassed, but rather than put him away, trifled with him, showing much skin. The referee called a halt after two rounds.

Mike Locke, middleweight wrestling champion of the world, took on John Anderson, Deseret Gym champ, for a ten minutes exhibition. Mike showed his class, demonstrating the effectiveness of many new holds.

Stein of Company II lost a three-round boxing bout to Fowler of the battery after taking severe drubbing. Fowler of the Deseret Gym went on with his classmate Parkins for a ten-minute wrestle; Harrington of the battery redeemed his past record by winning from Olcson of the signal corps in two fast rounds. This contest was scheduled for three sessions and Olcson led his man by far in the first, but Harrington, whipping lefts and rights to the stomach, forced the signal corps man to quit.

To wind up, two battery men went on in a blindfolded boxing match. This bout furnished much diversion, but the referee received the greater part of the blows and soon called a halt.

Luncheon was served and Lyle Smith furnished the musical numbers, singing recent song hits.

Wesley King made a brief speech and the audience dispersed, much pleased with the show.

Tallahassee, Dec 8.—State Superintendent Holloway has issued his biennial report of the schools of the state and a great deal of interesting data in connection herewith for the two years ending June 30th, 1912. The report covers a wide scope and in addition to general reports from the various counties of the progress and condition in their respective districts, there is a vast amount of statistical information which on studied gives a most comprehensive insight into school conditions in Florida.


The total enrolment of pupils for the state, both races, 151,120, or about 85 per cent of the school population of the state. The percentage of enrolment to population and the average daily attendance in proportion to enrolment are increasing. This is proof positive of growing interest in the value of education.


There are 2,701 schools in the state, 800 of which are white and 1,901 colored. The average length of the school term is 160 days or six months and nine days; whites 175 days and negroes 100.

There are 60 others who hold certificates for the various special classes. New York, May 10.—The Roosevelt committee today gave out the following copy of letter from Col. Theodore Roosevelt to Hon. R. A. Caswell of Minneapolis:


New York, May 10, 1912.
Hon. R. A. Caswell, chairman of the Roosevelt Committee and clerk of Supreme court, Minneapolis, Minn.


I wish it had been possible for me to go again to Minnesota. It is physically impossible. Nine states have now held presidential primaries, or their equivalent—North Dakota, Wisconsin, Illinois, Pennsylvania, Nebraska, Oregon, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Maryland. These states, the only ones in which there has been a free chance for the expression of the popular will, are to be represented by 256 delegates in the Chicago convention. Forty of these delegates are instructed for President Taft and 216 against him. He has carried but two of the nine states—New Hampshire and Massachusetts—which in Massachusetts the Roosevelt delegates at large were elected by over twice the majority which Mr. Taft obtained on the preferential vote. In Maryland the majority against Mr. Taft was about the same, proportionately, as the majorities for him in Massachusetts and New Hampshire. In the other seven states the margin, from one to twenty to one. In all the states together about three out of every four of the Republicans who voted at the primaries were against Mr. Taft. If primaries were held in all the states there would undoubtedly be no substantial variation from these figures, and Mr. Taft could by no possibility have 200 votes in the Chicago convention. Mr. Taft's chance of nomination lies solely in securing at Chicago, delegates who will misrepresent the will of the people. He can get the delegates, not in the primary states, but in the convention states, where delegates are chosen under the old system and even in these states he can only get them where the state is ruled by a boss.


After prolonged experience of me as president, practically all of the big bosses in the Republican party dislike me so heartily that they opposed Mr. Taft's nomination because I favored it. They were afraid that Mr. Taft would give them the same kind of trouble that I had given them. After three years and half experience of Mr. Taft since he has been elected, these same men have turned around and heartily favor his nomination. They were opposed to me four years ago and they are opposed to me now. They were opposed to Mr. Taft four years ago when they had not tried him as president and they heartily support him now. These men include, for instance, Mr. Gallinger in New Hampshire, Mr. Aldrich in Rhode Island, Mr. Penrose in Pennsylvania, Mr. Healing in Indiana, Mr. Lorimer in Illinois, Messrs. Guggenheim and Evans in Colorado, Mr. Calhoun and the Southern Pacific Railway group in California and the Amalgamated Copper crowd in Montana; and in your own state they include Mr. Smith and Mr. Tawney. The fight is a nationwide fight of the plain people against the bosses.


"There is just one candidate whom it is possible to nominate against the bosses and that is myself. To vote for every other candidate from now on is in reality vote for the bosses.

accommodation of visitors. The no

formally put before the board, it had

members for several years to inau-
gurate such a system for the con-

the fair with several children and
find it difficult to secure accommo-

the plan would be adopted by the
board at its next meeting.

bic tent at a reasonable cost.

Trip From Old Point.


Miss Bell Perkins is at home, 417
west Franklin Street, after spending
several delightful weeks at Old Point.
The early spring season is always
charming at this celebrated coast re-
sort, and never more so than at pres-
ent.


To Spend Easter at Horn Quarter.


Dr. Edward Rowe, of Stamford,
Conn., his son and daughter will com-
e to Virginia to spend Easter at their
new home, Horn Quarter, in Hanover
county.


Sir and Mrs. H. B. Smith left Rich-
mond yesterday for Horn Quarter to
put everything in order for the com-
ing occupancy of the new owners of the place.
Mrs. Smith will go to లewisburg, Va. for
the Easter holidays, to be with her
son, Forester, who is at school near
Lewisburg. Afterward she will spend
some time at Ashland, Va., while Mr.
Smith is in Florida looking after some
landed interests there.


Dinner Parties and Weddings.


Miss Belle Willard was guest of
honor Saturday evening at dinner
party given by her friend and hostess,
Miss Elizabeth Hopkins, at the Balti-
more Country Club.


Dr. and Mrs. Christopher Francis
Newbill, of Essex county, have sent
invitations for the marriage of
their daughter, Katherine Trippe New-
bill, to Charles the wedding to
be celebrated Tuesday evening, April

Invitations have been issued by Mr.
and Mrs. Thomas Christian Gordon for
the marriage of their niece, Martha
Gordon Lescuyve to Mason White, in
All Saints Church, Thursday, April
11, at 4 o'clock p. m.


Married in Oxford.


News has just reached Richmond of
the marriage in Oxford, Va., last
Friday of Miss Edna C. Harding, of On-
tario, Va., and Luther Turner, for many
years and at present associated with
the post office at Richmond.


Mrs. Swanson Honored.


On the anniversary of the signing of the
treaty of Ghent, the National Associa-
tion, Daughters of the American Revo-
lution, has complimented Mrs. Claude
A. Swanson, of Virginia and Wash-
ington, D. C., by making her chair-
man of a committee from the Daugh-
ters which will arrange the program
for the celebration. Mrs. Matthew R.
Scott, President-General of the or-
ganization, will assist the committee.


Called Meeting.


The board of managers of the Home
for Incurables will hold a called meet-
ing at 2 p. m. to-day in the home.


Monthly Meeting of DANES.


The Virginia Society of Colonial
Danes will hold its monthly meeting
Friday afternoon, March 20, at 4
o'clock, in the parlors of Woman's
Club.


To Hold a Dinner Dance.


The Tuesday Evening German Club
will meet next Tuesday evening to
give a dinner dance, with German
figures, Mr. Starnell, of Washington,
D. C., leading. Dancing will begin at
9 o'clock and end at 11.

Special To The Times-Dispatch.

Asheville, N. C., October 13.—The directors of the Asheville County Club at a recent meeting authorised in preparation of $500 for improvements to the clubhouse, while it was decided to spend $1,000 on improving the eighteen-hole golf-course. The club house will be made modern in every detail, and will complete one of the handsomest in the State. At the annual meeting of the stockholders, held during the latter part of the week, the following men were chosen directors: Thomas Wadley Raoul, G. C. Millard, W. S. Randolph, A. G. Barnard and J. H. Brown, who elected the following officers for the coming year: president Thomas W. Raoul; vice-president G. C. Millard; secretary W. S. Randolph; treasurer J. L. Ewen.

Seventy members of the American Geographical Society, who have been making a tour of a number of the States of the Union in a special train, spent Friday here. The visitors were met at the local Southern passenger station by a party of Asheville business and professional men and were driven to the principal points of interest in and around the city. Shortly before noon, they were taken to the summit of Sunset Mountain, where they were the guests of C. W. Grove at lunch.

The Asheville Lodge of Elks is contemplating the erection of a new home at the corner of Walnut and Haywood Streets, and at the next meeting of the board of directors of the Elks' Home Company, a request will be made that they be given the authority to sell four lots from the company's property and issue bonds for the erection of the building. At present the Elks occupy a handsome home on a large lot. The building formerly was used as a private dwelling house. The company contemplates selling a part of the property for residences or business houses and using the proceeds for the erection of the new home.

The local council of the United Commercial Travellers entertained the friends and customers of its members Thursday night at an elaborate spread, which was attended by about seventy-five merchants from various towns of Western North Carolina. The principal address was delivered by Locke Craig, Democratic nominee for Governor, who was introduced by W. R. Bearden. Other addresses were delivered by Manager Sanford H. Cohen, of the Greater Western North Carolina Association, and Secretary Neptune Buckner, of the Asheville Board of Trade.

Department Commander John A. Gundy, of the Spanish-American war veterans, has appointed the following North Carolinians who will represent this State on the staff of the commander-in-chief of the United States: R. E. Steele, of Lumberton; Harold E. Johnson, of Asheville; Dr. Thomas E. Struggled, of Waynesville. The men appointed by the department commander have been officially notified of their appointments. Within the past few weeks a number of camps have been organized in this State, and an effort is being made to form them in each town which has a sufficient number of veterans to justify the granting of a charter.

Asheville's city prison has been completed, and is now being used for the confinement of prisoners. The prison, situated on the south side of the City Hall, is fireproof and adjoins the Police Court chamber. Work on the structure has been in progress for the past three months, during which time the Buncombe County Jail has been used for the confinement of persons charged with violating city ordinances.

About twenty members of the Greek colony here have left Asheville for New York to set sail for the land of their nativity and bear arms against Turkey. About fifty men of this nationality have been engaged in various lines of business here for years past, and some of those who have left have amassed small fortunes during their residence in this city. In the majority of cases the Greeks have conducted restaurants and pool rooms, which have been leased to other business men, in order that their owners may become soldiers.

The second annual Western North Carolina Fair, which began last Thursday, closed Friday night. It was a success from every point of view, and the directors are greatly pleased with the support which they received. The exhibits were many and varied, and the judging was a difficult task. The show was featured by numerous free attractions, including a horse show, an automobile obstacle race and several events, which were pulled off on the Midway. Joyner and Commissioner of Agriculture W. A. Graham.

C., January 2.—Before Congress has been in session many days there will be a temporary suspension of talk regarding presidential candidates, the Sherwood pension bill, the intellectual efforts made by a few members to cut down the mileage grab and kindred subjects, and strict attention will be paid to other matters. Regular committee hearings have already begun. Chairman Hay, of the House Military Affairs Committee, is busy getting his measure for the consolidation of several departments of the army in shape; Chairman Padgett, of the Naval Affairs Committee, is beginning figuring on how to build for the country one or two big battleships at the least possible cost; the Judiciary people will wrestle with that ever-recurring wins Key problem and a law that will keep rum out of dry territory; the Post Office and Post Roads Committee will begin regular hearings to regulate the country's big posts business, and, in fact, everything will be in full swing all along the line before the end of the present week.

For a while after the Jackson Day events, political here at least for the present, political issues will be sidetracked in order that the real business for which Congress assembled may be transacted.

The Jackson Day dinner over, and the time and place for holding the next Democratic national convention agreed upon, the country may expect six or seven months of good hard work at the hands of the nation's lawmakers.

Within two days an employers liability bill will be introduced in the Senate and the House. The special commission appointed some time ago to investigate and report upon this work has, after months of labor, completed its hearings, and will now ask Congress to act upon its recommendations.

The two bills will be drawn for the House and Senate by Congressman Brantley, of Georgia, and Senator Sutherland, of Utah. While in the opinion of Senator Sutherland such a law would entail an expenditure of about 100,000 annually, it is his opinion also that this would probably be counterbalanced by reduction in court expenses.

The proposed law would provide for a graduated scale of damages based on the nature of the injuries received by the employee.

It is generally agreed by both the labor interests and the railroads that a law of the kind contemplated is needed.

Another important measure that will receive consideration soon is the establishment of Children's Bureau, for the purpose of improving conditions in child life generally.

Advocates of the measure take the position that inasmuch as the Federal government appropriates literally to study animal life, the soil, entomology and kindred subjects, some attention should be given the matter of collecting information and statistics on infant mortality, race degeneracy and the health and training of children.

Senator Borah, of Idaho, is taking great interest in the movement to collect all available information regarding the life, habits and general characteristics of children from various viewpoints, and Congressman Peters, of Massachusetts, is equally interested in the matter in the House.

It is estimated that the operation of a bureau such as that contemplated would not cost more than 100,000 a year, and it is pointed out that the United States cannot afford to be niggardly when millions are spent to protect property rights alone.

it to the third, under the lewdly
sculptured arch of which he stopped

time Kathiapur the Fallen was re-
vealed to him in the awful beauty of
its naked desolation.

A wide and stately avenue stretched
away from the portals, between rows

stone, tombstones and mausoleums
with meaner houses of sun-dried brick
and rubble, roofless all and disinte-
grating in the slow, terrible process

alert ghosts rose from the under
growth and scurried silently thence:
a circumstance which made him very
unhappy.

imitation of a badly wounded man

edge of broken sandstone tomb. The

himself unexpectedly in the middle of

paces down the street, then paused
and beckoned him with a gaunt arm.

had that gun."

native swathed in black from his head
to his heels and seemed the more
strikingly peculiar in view of the fact
that, as far as Amber could deter
mine, he had neither eyes nor features
although his head was without any
sort of covering. He gulped over the
proposition for an instant, then
stepped forward.

"Evidently my appointed cicerone,"
he considered. "Unquestionably this
ghost-dance is excellently stage-man-
aged. Though, of course, had
to pick out that particular tomb."

He followed in the wake of the fig-
ure, which sped on with a singular
motion, something between a walk
and a glide, conscious that his eu-
animity had been restored rather than
shaken by the incident.

shadow, passing forsaken temples and
lordly pleasure houses, all marble
tracery and fretwork, standing apart

and cots on whose hearthstones the
fires for centuries had been cold—his
destination evidently the temple of
the unspeakable Eye.

As they drew nearer the leading

which he seemed to favor, sweeping
hastily across a plaza white with
moon-glare and without pause on into
the black, gaping hole beyond the

back, stopping score of feet from
the door, his nerves a-jangle. He did
not falter in his purpose; he was go-
ing to enter the inky portal, but
would he ever leave it? And
the world was sweet to him.

He took firm hold of his reason and
went on across the dark threshold,

Western Newspaper Union News Service

Little Rock.—State Auditor John K. Lobe made his biennial report to the governor last week. He makes several recommendations for changes and improvements in some of the state departments and institutions.

In speaking of the state's financial condition Mr. Lobe gives some strong facts and figures. He says that the present taxable value of the state is something in excess of $425,000,000, an increase of about $50,000,000 in the last two years, estimating the state's income for the next two years on this basis, combined with the revenue from all sources, will give the state a sum of $2,272,063.75 for all state purposes. Mr. Lobe says this would have been enough to run the state on an economical basis for the next two years if it was not for the fact that the state had issued a great amount of scrip in the last two years and that this will have to be paid out of future revenues unless the legislature makes some other provisions for the caring of the scrip debts.

According to Mr. Lobe, for several months past the state has been meeting its debts promptly but the treasury will soon be without funds again and the state will have to return to the scrip basis again.

This state of Arkansas finances is due, Mr. Lobe says, to the legislature making appropriations without investigating the state's ability to meet the obligations placed upon it by these appropriations.

In the report Auditor Lobe strongly recommends a change in the management of the state penitentiary.

At the present time the penitentiary is under the control of a board composed of five state officials. Mr. Lobe says that while the penitentiary has been a success and self sustaining under the present plan of management that it could be more efficiently managed under the supervision of a man or men who could devote their entire time to the affairs of the penitentiary. The financial affairs of the penitentiary are good and when the present crop is sold all debts will be paid and a surplus left to begin the new year on.

In treating of the state pension roll the report says that the roll has been growing continually but that the increase in the pension revenue has kept pace with the growing roll.

The report recommends that as nearly all the pensioners are now drawing $100 a year from the state that $100 be made the uniform rate of all pensions.

President Taft's friends will control the state convention of Ohio and will elect six at-large who will support the President in the national convention at Chicago, the statement says. While Mr. Roosevelt will have majority of the district delegates, President Taft has carried the state convention by a substantial majority, indicating that he is as much entitled to claim the state as Mr. Roosevelt. The Ohio outcome emphasizes the existing incongruities of the present primary laws. Among the peculiar developments of these primaries during the present campaign, in addition to Ohio, have been the following:

Jointly, as a Fourth of July celebration and means of raising funds for the benefit of the district, the Osborne Parent Teacher Association will give an ice cream social on the evening of the Fourth. This was decided at a meeting of the circle last Wednesday afternoon, and to complete arrangements for the affair Mrs. W. I. A. Wilson, the president, will call a special meeting later in the month.

Club women throughout the country will follow with interest the Biennial Convention proceedings. Many clubs have joined the federation since the Boston convention, attended by 1900 delegates, and it is believed that the San Francisco convention greatly will exceed that record. Suffrage has not been given a place on the official program, but nonetheless it will be introduced when on July a special demonstration is being planned by the California women.

Mrs. L. L. Blankenburg, second vice president of the general federation and wife of Philadelphia's reform mayor, is now in California. In a recent interview she said: "I consider Women's clubs the greatest of training schools for woman's citizenship. The very motto of the general federation, Unity in Diversity, explains what a broadening influence federation work has upon women. They grow to realize that they need not all be of the same belief and creed, politics or other matters, in order to get together and work for certain questions and improvements which they believe will be of greatest good to humanity."

In celebration of the Fourth of July, the Madison Improvement club will give a picnic to the members and their families on the grounds surrounding the home of Mrs. H. G. Brooks. A patriotic program will be presented during the afternoon. The club will meet once a month until autumn when it will resume its weekly sessions.

Undaunted by defeats in the past, the suffragists will again go before the national republican convention to request the insertion of an equal suffrage plank in the party platform. The time for this move has not yet been decided upon, but the interview will take place in the committee room of the committee on resolutions at as late a date as possible, as it is desired to include in the suffrage delegation as many prominent visiting advocates of the cause as possible.

same time it improves the land.

"It was our intention," said Justice Collins, "to spell out the original intention of those who drafted the law. We, the District Attorney and the bench of Special Sessions, do not consider ourselves empowered to do general legislative work, but in this particular instance we feel that owing to the necessarily strict interpretation of the law the design of its originators has been nullified.

From the penalties attached to other violations of the law, such as not to exceed $500 for violation of the so-called speeding section, the fine of $50 for violation of certain sections relating to registration by manufacturers and dealers, the fine of $50 for the chauffeur who has no license, it is evident that the makers of the law intended that the punishment for a drunken chauffeur should be that of the ordinary misdemeanant—a possible year in prison, with a fine of not more than $500.

My personal opinion is that no one should be allowed to drive a full engine as is the modern automobile through the streets of a great city unless he has proved his proficiency. The engineer of the locomotive, which is confined to a track of steel rails, has to be a skilled man; he has to show his competence. How much more should the chauffeur who drives his engine through crowded streets be compelled to pass an efficiency test?

I think that such tests should be made compulsory for every driver of an automobile, whether he be owner or chauffeur. That, of course, is merely my private opinion. I am not a legislator."

The draft of the proposed amendment was taken by Justice Collins to Edward J. McGoldrick, of the Corporation Counsel's office, the legal representative in Albany of the city of New York. Mr. McGoldrick agreed with Justice Collins that it was a matter of grave public importance. He promised that it would be speedily introduced in the Senate and the Assembly and that he would see Governor Sulzer personally and ask that the usual formalities which delay bills in the Legislature be removed, so that it could be passed upon with expedition. Justice Collins said that he saw no reason why the amendment should not become law within a week after the Legislature convened.

No provision is made in the proposed amendments for the substitution of a prison sentence for those who cannot pay their fines. The justices of Special Sessions came to the conclusion, after the Marley case, that the general provision of the penal law, which makes it possible to impose one day's imprisonment for every dollar of the fine unpaid, applies to offenders against the Callan law, as to all other offenders. In the future no one will walk out as Marley did.

Magistrate Herbert, in the Essex Market police court, yesterday, being in doubt as to whether he could punish chauffeur under the Callan law for reckless driving and running down patrolman, sent the chauffeur to Blackwell's Island for six months for disorderly conduct. He also took occasion to say that some punishment must be devised at once to meet cases of daredevil driving.

John Ryan, a chauffeur in the employ of William Pierce, of Englewood, N. J., ran down Patrolman Phair at Third street and the Bowery early yesterday morning. Phair was badly bruised about the head and shoulders by being thrown against a pillar of the elevated road. He arrested Ryan and arraigned him before Magistrate Herbert. Phair said that Ryan was driving at the rate of forty miles an hour. After striking him, Phair said Ryan drove his car into a northbound streetcar with such force as to break several of the windows in the car and injure his own steering gear. It was owing to this mishap that Ryan was caught.

Ryan said that he was following a slowly moving northbound car, and that when the car stopped he turned out to pass it and struck Phair, who was directly in its path.

"Although the statement is made that Ryan's car struck the officer," said Magistrate Herbert, "and then hit a streetcar, and that Ryan used abusive language to Phair, I am unable, according to a recent decision of a higher court on the Callan law, to entertain the charge. But the law does give me the power to entertain a charge of disorderly conduct against Ryan, and I direct the officer to make such a charge."

Ryan was found guilty and sent to the workhouse for five months and twenty nine days, with an additional fine of $51 because the front lights of his car were not lighted.

Goshen, N. Y., September 30.—Dr.
Otto H. Schultze, of New York, a coroner's
physician, took the witness stand
this afternoon in the preliminary examination
of Burton W. Gibson, and
testified that Mrs. Rosa Menschik
Szabo, with whose death Gibson was
charged, died of strangulation by
compression on the throat and not
of drowning. Upon his testimony District
Attorney Rogers declared the
state's case must stand or fall.


Dr. Schultz testified as to the autopsy
he performed on Mrs. Szabo's body
where Gibson, who was the woman's
lawyer, had ordered it buried in Jersey
City. Adjournment was reached with
Dr. Schultz on the stand. Dr. J. J.
O'Reilly, professor of medico-legal
at St. Lawrence University
here, to combat for Gibson the
theory that Mrs. Szabo did not die of
drowning, in a statement said:


Dr. Schultz's testimony was learned
and a beautiful lecture. His analysis
showed that death could have been
due to any of half dozen or more
causes, including heart disease, acute
indigestion, uraemia, and drowning;
thousands of persons have drowned
without inhaling water. It fits in
beautifully with the defense.


Several state witnesses preceded
Mr. Schultz. John Minturn, store
keeper near Greenwood Lake, in
whose water Mrs. Szabo died, testi-
fied that Gibson and his companion
were exchanging places at the moment
their boat tipped over. He declared
that he saw the boat rock and cap-
size, the struggle in the water, the
reappearance of the man above the
surface and his clinging to the craft
as it drifted away.


William Krompf, of Rutherford, N.
J., was 500 feet away in his motor boat
when the boat capsized. He heard
Gibson yell, inarticulately, and soon
was beside him. "Don't mind me,
here is a lady there; look for her," he
said Gibson shouted as he neared the
capsized craft. Krompf pulled Gibson
aboard his boat which remained on
the spot for ten minutes while her
crew of three scanned the water for
Gibson's companion.


Albert McDaniel, whose rowboat
Gibson hired, declared that Mrs. Szabo
wanted to take the water in canoe
but he told her it would probably up-
set. He told Gibson to take a safer
boat. Gibson said tonight that he
expected to be held for the grand jury
but was confident he would win his
freedom on a trial. Everybody
who had testified to-day told the truth, he
added, but Dr. Schultz was in error in
his conclusions.

Thanks People of Hawaii.


"Tell the people of Hawaii for me that I feel more than I can express my gratitude to all for their kindness during these months and the warm aloha welcome given me today on my return to dear old Honolulu and my native Hawaii," said Kahanamoku.


"It was too bad that I was alone over in Europe for many people would ask me any amount of questions about this city and the Islands and it was impossible for me to answer everything and everybody.


"Say, but it feels good to get back to Hawaii again. I had a pleasant time every moment since I left Honolulu eight months ago and everybody treated me well.


"Do you want to go to the next Olympic meeting?" was asked him.


"Yes, if I may. Hawaii can have a team there which will beat the world.


Poi and Royalty.


"Poi!" and Duke gulped, "Well I had the first taste of real poi at home this morning after landing. I tasted something like poi in New York when I came across Benny Jones and the Bird Of Paradise people one evening but it was a tame article alongside the real thing."


From poi, the reporter skipped royalty and asked Duke how many crowned heads he had met over in Europe.


"Con, well, I met two or three kings and crown princes. I am sure I saw a king and another queen; the other was a crown prince of some shore, but I forget." An unaffected and astonishing reply from the lad whom the royalty had inclined by the hand and honored when he won say into one of the world's most coveted athletic titles.

and to occupy afterward is nearly
square, of medium size, full two sto-
ries in height, with a good, deep cel-
lar and an attic big enough to act as
buffer against heat in summer and
cold in winter. Such houses give
more room according to the size of
the foundation and roof than any other
design.

that work to good advantage. There
are certain geometrical combinations
that work to a disadvantage in a
square house, but are easily overcome
when you add a few feet to the
length.


One of the difficulties is the stair
way, which interferes with the proper
laying-out of the rooms in every short
house. Stairways in dwelling houses
have caused more gray hairs, and sent
more architects to early graves, than
any other feature in house building.
There was a time when a rough lad-
der fashioned with an axe answered
the purpose. It was made with the
trunks of two trees for sides, and sec-
tions of smaller trees for rungs.
There was a hole through the upper
floor and usually an effort was made
to place the opening where the roof
was high enough so you could not miss
hitting the knots on the rafters with
your head. From that time to this,
stairways have grown in complexity
until we think we have them about
perfect.

Out of the dust of discussion in Congress, more especially in the House, this session, two facts are pretty clearly apparent, bearing on the parcels post and the future of the express companies in the United States.

One of these is that the establishment of a parcels post system is seemingly certain to come eventually. The other is that the express companies are going to be put out of business.

At one time, it looked much as if the Cooke bill, whereby the Government would purchase the express companies, would be passed by the House. But it will not be. All the indications now are that the plan for the Government to take over the express companies is made to appear extremely doubtful. This fact and the assertion that the express companies seeing parcels post coming, would like nothing better than to be taken over by the general government, have put a damper on the movement to purchase the express companies. It is pretty clear that many of the members who have given divers reasons for not wanting the Government to take over the express companies are mated by fear that for the Government to operate the express companies would be the beginning of Government ownership of railroads. At the same time that the Government would get badly "stung" if it took over the express companies at anything like the values that have been mostly suggested.

Mr. Martin has strongly urged a proposition in the House that has substantial support. It is that the railroads of the country shall hereafter perform the entire express business, up to eleven pounds or whatever limit weight might be established by the Government, and that they shall be completely under the control of the Interstate Commerce Commission.

He pointed out in debate that a package started on rural route to some destination could be stamped with the amount required to transport it on the rural route and also with the amount needed for its hauling as an express package by the railroads. This plan Mr. Martin urged, would obviate Government ownership of the express companies.

Just how the express proposition and the parcels post question are going to be worked out is not easy to tell, but the feeling is deep set in Congress that the two things must be met. Senator Bourne has put into the Senate a parcels post bill, based on a zone or distance system, and this has much support. Many predict a bill of this sort will eventually go through, though probably not this session. The solution of this business may be that the express is along the lines to establish a parcels post based on a zone or distance system; and in this connection to require the railroads to do the express business. The operation of this plan, it is urged, would be greatly to reduce the cost of carrying parcels. Congress is not yet in a mood to adopt a plan for a general unlimited system of parcels post where parcels would be carried for the same sums regardless of distance, though Congressman Sulzer insists this is the true principle, and the plan is steadily gaining in favor and will be adopted eventually.

Indianapolis, Ind. October 10.—For the first
time since he confessed to dynamiting, Mc나ugal
before a jury in the dynamite
conspiracy trial to-day was identified by
hotel clerks as having visited various cities
at times when explosions occurred.


H. T. Pearce, Kansas City, was in the
pages of hotel registers traced at W. H.
City Hotel August 20, 1870, three days before
McNamara blew up a portion of $1,000,000
bridge across the Missouri River, which he
says, was arranged for by W. Bert Brown,
of Kansas City, and James McNamara.


Pearce identified McNamara in the court
room. The line of testimony was
followed by the government, tending to
carry out McNamara's confession that he
actually caused the explosions detailed in his
confession, and for which the government
charges members of the executive board of
the International Association of Bridge and
Structural Iron Workers paid him at the
rate of $200 job.


J. Quigley, of Duluth, Minn., identified
McNamara as a visitor at a Duluth hotel
in July, 1910, shortly before an explosion at
Superior, Wis.


J. U. Gates said McNamara was the W.
G. Bly, who frequently registered at a
hotel at Rochester, Pa., near which later
were uncovered quantities of nitro-glycerine
hidden in a shed.

his return to Indiana polls after blowing up
the Times building also were traced in hotel
ledgers. At the suggestion of his brother,
James P. took the name of Frank Sullivan,
dropping all the aliases he had used
on the Pacific Coast.

which were identified by managers of sales-
offices from many parts of the country,
but contents of which were withheld
until later, government attorneys announced
it would be shown that arrangements for the
Pacific Coast explosions were carried on by
telegraph; that Olaf Tveismoe and Eugene

and Munsey worried over the search and
investigated for the dynamiters, sent back
telegrams concerning the whereabouts
of James B. McNamara.

Sweet potatoes need to be handled

through the winter, and unlike most
other vegetables, sweet potatoes
should be kept in warm, dry place.


In the first place sweet potatoes
must be dug at the right time. They
should be dug before the frosts have
killed the tops for this Injuries the
quality of the tubers somewhat


After digging, the potatoes must be
handled as carefully as though they
were eggs. Irish potatoes can be

often a bruise in one OF the potatoes,
or even decayed spot will not af-
feet the other part which is left in
sound condition.

quality of the sound portion at the
other end and will render it unfit for
use This fact is not generally under
stood by many growers who handle
sweet potatoes as carelessly as they
do Irish potatoes.

the potatoes of poor quality which are
served during the winter.

place. temperature of 60 to 70 de-
grees is about right for the proper
keeping of sweet potatoes.


Some persons have stored them in
THE sand or dust from the country
road to help preserve an even TEN
perature,


If the potatoes are stored In sand or
dust, care must be taken that the
sand Is perfectly dry.


Handled carefully, sweet potatoes
can be kept for some months and will
be found of good quality late in the
winter.

Special Correspondence,

BRANDYWINE SUMMIT CAMP.
Pa., Aug. 20.--The spirit of good fellowship and cordiality that has characterized the camp of 1912 culminated last night in the speeches of thanks at the final tabernacle meeting, in the walk around, and the serenades following the formal closing. In the appreciations given the camp officials, the audience, composed of all the tenters on the grounds and a goodly number of visitors, gave hearty endorsement, saying nothing too good could be said of all who have helped with the camp. Professor W. N. Thomas, who had to leave in the morning, received praise that showed he had won the respect and affection of everyone, and the audience heard with pleasure that he will return next year. A pouring rain fell during the tabernacle meeting, and destroyed a good many of the lighted Japanese lanterns strung oil over the grounds, but the rain stopped in time for the walk around and multitudes of candies and red and green fire and sparklers made up for the shortage in lanterns.

The Rev. T. F. Beauchamp was the first speaker. He said that the results of the camp season were beyond his most sanguine expectation, his work as preacher-in-charge had been a delight because of the splendid men and women helping, and he had made more acquaintances at camp than in the time he has been in Wilmington.

He praised the Rev. Blair S. Latshaw, saying his young peoples' services had been perhaps the most popular in camp. Dr. J. D. G. Hanna, the superintendent, the Board of Trustees, his brother preachers, had stood by him in every possible way. He said that if camp had done nothing more than hold the children's meetings conducted by Aubrey Vandeyer, they would have been worth all the work. He said the musical director, W. N. Thomas was one of the great men of the country, and they hoped to have him in Wilmington churches next winter. Mr. Beauchamp missed but one service, when he was called into town for wedding, and so faithful were the program preachers that only two breaks in the program occurred and these were promptly filled by other preachers. The Rev. Blair S. Latshaw spoke of the invaluable friendships formed in the camp, and said he, too, had met more strangers than in all the time he had been in Wilmington.

Vanderbilt hotel has vanished from the
face of the earth. Large men with broad
shoulders now sit before the buffet which
was once dedicated to the feminine, and
wreaths of the incense of perfumes linger
among the rare old Chinese paintings on
the walls of that retreat. The English
butler who was wont to serve dainty
drinks and creme violette and curacao in
thin-stemmed glasses now is content to
purvey the Scotch highball of commerce.


It was decided several days ago by the
management to abolish the bar for the
fair, because the idea did not seem to
find especial favor in their eyes. It was
only an experiment, an innovation. One
changes chairs about a new hotel from
this corner to that and moves rugs about
and hangs the pictures first on that wall
and then on this. So it was that the
woman's bar, with its Chippendale chairs
of the Cathay influence, and its blue and
yellow rugs, its grin work in the windows,
has been transmitted into a cafe where
one may have a cocktail, chat with a
friend and be gone to other realms, brush-
ing one's high top hat on the way.
